anchorClaim: In low-income countries from 2010-2020, reductions of 20% or more in international vaccine funding correlate at r>=0.5 with declines in national vaccination coverage rates within 2 years.
dataQualityNote: Only 4 real datoms exist for this claim against a sources_target of 100, a genuinely thin evidence base; the confidence_band (Speculative) and low score (0.11) reflect that honestly. None of the 4 retrieved sources directly measures the nucleus claim's specific quantitative relationship (20% funding cut correlating at r>=0.5 with coverage decline within 2 years): one paper (Berman 2004) predates the 2010-2020 study window, one (Lewnard 2020) measures vaccine effectiveness rather than funding-coverage links, one (Bruni 2020) documents a coverage-pattern trend without funding data, and one (Sbarra/LBD 2020) touches funding only as one of four co-named drivers (alongside conflict, vaccine scepticism, and supply disruption) behind a documented coverage slowdown, not as an independently tested predictor of it. Also worth flagging: the datomerId field stored on all 4 of the 4 individual datom records (44535375-36ad-4e00-9450-6b8936d9aee9 on three, f44ce3cf-a04f-4766-9d2f-db38f1800889 on one) does not match the parent Datomer's own datomerId (458642d5-4d7e-4840-89c9-081c23ccd489); linkage was confirmed instead via the Datomer's explicit datom_ids array and matching projectId (6391d547-4160-4938-bbba-ca770f16cde7), so a direct GSI query on datomerId returned zero rows.

datoms.claim: The paper does not measure the correlation between international vaccine funding reductions and vaccination coverage rate declines in low-income countries during 2010-2020.
datoms.source: P. Berman. "Immunization financing in developing countries and the international vaccine market: trends and issues" (2004). doi:10.1590/S0042-96862004000900017
datoms.domain: Public health policy and immunization financing
datoms.measure: Immunization financing trends and vaccine market dynamics
datoms.notes: Published in 2004, predating the 2010-2020 window specified in the nucleus claim; does not measure the funding-coverage correlation. Sample size not reported; flagged with a statistical-reliability warning during ingestion.

datoms.claim: Low- and middle-income countries with HPV vaccination programs achieved lower final-dose coverage rates than high-income countries due to higher dropout rates between first and final doses.
datoms.source: Laia Bruni, Anna Saura-Lázaro, Alexandra Montoliu, María Brotons, Laia Alemany. "HPV vaccination introduction worldwide and WHO and UNICEF estimates of national HPV immunization coverage 2010-2019" (2020). doi:10.1016/j.ypmed.2020.106399
datoms.population: Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and high-income countries with HPV vaccination programs, 2010-2019
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage rates (first dose and final dose)
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of WHO/UNICEF vaccination coverage estimates
datoms.notes: Addresses coverage outcomes in low-income settings but does not examine funding data or the relationship between funding reductions and coverage declines. Global population-weighted final-dose coverage was only 15% in 2019; only 6% of countries reached >90% final-dose coverage.

datoms.claim: The paper does not measure the correlation between international vaccine funding reductions and vaccination coverage declines; it measures vaccine effectiveness against antibiotic-treated illness outcomes.
datoms.source: Joseph A. Lewnard, Nathan C. Lo, Nimalan Arinaminpathy, Isabel Frost, Ramanan Laxminarayan. "Childhood vaccines and antibiotic use in low- and middle-income countries" (2020). doi:10.1038/s41586-020-2238-4
datoms.population: Children under five years of age in low- and middle-income countries
datoms.measure: Antibiotic-treated acute respiratory infection and diarrhoea episodes prevented by vaccination
datoms.methodology: Case-control study with household survey data
datoms.sample_size: 65,815 children from case-control analysis; 944,173 children across 77 countries in incidence analysis
datoms.notes: Measures vaccine effectiveness against antibiotic-treated illness, not the funding-to-coverage relationship in the nucleus claim; scored as contradicting because it is off-target to the claim rather than confirming it. Relied on mother-reported outcomes rather than standardized clinical assessment.

datoms.claim: In low-income and middle-income countries, measles vaccination coverage declined or stagnated in more than half of districts between 2010 and 2019, following gains from 2000 to 2010.
datoms.source: Local Burden of Disease Vaccine Coverage Collaborators, Alyssa N. Sbarra, Sam Rolfe, Jason Q. Nguyen, Lucas Earl. "Mapping routine measles vaccination in low- and middle-income countries" (2020). doi:10.1038/s41586-020-03043-4
datoms.population: Children aged 12-59 months in 101 low- and middle-income countries
datoms.methodology: Geostatistical modelling with Bayesian hierarchical framework
datoms.notes: Documents a slowdown in coverage progress after 2010 (70.5% of districts improving 2000-2010 versus only 40.1% in 2010-2019), which authors attribute to conflict, vaccine scepticism, funding support, and supply disruptions jointly, not funding withdrawal in isolation. Cites Angola's 28% drop in per-capita health spending (2010-2018) coinciding with coverage declines as one example among several drivers.

methodologyMix.label: Cross-sectional analysis of WHO/UNICEF vaccination coverage estimates

guide.whatScienceSays: DATOM located just 4 real datoms for this claim, far short of the corpus this claim needs. Of those 4, 0% (0 of 4) directly support the stated funding-to-coverage relationship, 25% (1 of 4) is scored as contradicting, and 75% (3 of 4) are only conditionally relevant, and not one of the four was actually designed to test the claim as stated: a 20%-or-greater international funding cut correlating at r>=0.5 with a national coverage decline within two years. The geostatistical mapping study from the Local Burden of Disease Vaccine Coverage Collaborators, drawing on 1,697,570 children across 354 household surveys in 101 low- and middle-income countries, documents that measles coverage improved in 70.5% of districts from 2000-2010 but in only 40.1% from 2010-2019, and it names Angola's 28% drop in per-capita health spending from 2010-2018 as one example coinciding with that slowdown, but the authors attribute the broader pattern jointly to conflict, vaccine scepticism, funding support, and supply disruptions, not to funding withdrawal in isolation. The source scored as 'contradicting,' Lewnard et al. 2020, earns that label not because it refutes the claim but because it measures something else entirely: vaccine effectiveness against antibiotic-treated illness, studied in 65,815 children in a case-control analysis and 944,173 children across 77 countries in an incidence analysis. The remaining two sources, a 2004 policy literature review that predates the claim's 2010-2020 window and a 2020 cross-sectional analysis of HPV coverage across 107 countries (where global final-dose coverage reached only 15% in 2019), round out a set that documents vaccination-equity patterns generally without ever pairing a funding-level change to a coverage outcome.
guide.howConfident: It would be a mistake to read the 0% direct-support figure as if DATOM were reporting near-certainty that the claim is false: the confidence score is 11% ('Speculative'), not 0%, and that gap runs in an unusual direction for this evidence base. Normally a majority of supporting studies inflates a confidence score beyond what quality alone would justify; here it is the near-total absence of on-target studies (0 of 4 supports, 3 of 4 only conditionally relevant) that keeps the score in single digits rather than driving it all the way to zero, because DATOM's scoring distinguishes 'no evidence found for this specific mechanism' from 'evidence found and it actively refutes the mechanism.' None of the 4 retrieved sources tested the funding-cut-to-coverage-decline relationship at the correlation strength (r>=0.5) or the two-year time horizon the claim specifies, so there is nothing here to falsify, only tangential material to weigh cautiously. That tangential material is also structurally weak for building confidence: the 4 datoms span 4 different methodologies with zero overlap between them, meaning no single finding has been independently replicated even once; the source base splits evenly between TEXT_NO_METADATA and PDF_FULL_TEXT extraction, with the two metadata-thin sources including the one study outside the 2010-2020 window; and the total pool of 4 sits at just 4% of the 100-source target DATOM set for this claim, well below the volume needed to distinguish a real pattern from noise. Read the 11% as 'not enough has been found here to say anything with confidence,' not as 'the evidence leans against this.'
decisionSupport: Do not cite the r>=0.5 funding-to-coverage-decline correlation as evidenced: none of the 4 retrieved datoms measured that relationship directly, and the corpus sits at just 4% of its 100-source target for this claim.

The one directly relevant coverage-slowdown pattern in this evidence base (measles MCV1 progress falling from 70.5% of improving districts in 2000-2010 to only 40.1% in 2010-2019, across 101 low- and middle-income countries) is real and documented, but its authors attribute it jointly to conflict, vaccine scepticism, funding support, and supply disruption, not to funding cuts in isolation; do not isolate funding as the driver.

Treat the Angola example cited in that same study (a 28% drop in per-capita health spending from 2010-2018 coinciding with coverage decline) as a single illustrative data point inside a broader mapping study, not as a tested funding-coverage correlation.

If this claim needs to inform a real decision, commission or locate studies that pair quantified national funding changes with coverage outcomes directly; none of the 4 methodologies present here (literature review, cross-sectional coverage-estimate analysis, case-control household survey, Bayesian geostatistical modelling) was designed for that pairing.

Discount the Lewnard 2020 'contradicts' flag as evidence against the claim: it is scored that way because it is off-target, measuring vaccine effectiveness against antibiotic-treated illness in 65,815 to 944,173 children, not because it found data refuting a funding-coverage link.
guide.faultLines: Corpus Thinness: at 4 real datoms against a 100-source target for this claim (4% of goal), this evidence base has nowhere near the volume DATOM needs to separate a real signal from noise, and the Speculative band with an 11% score is the honest arithmetic consequence of that shortfall rather than a verdict on the claim's truth. Methodological Non-Replication: the 4 datoms were produced by 4 entirely different methodologies (literature review and policy analysis, cross-sectional WHO/UNICEF coverage analysis, case-control household survey, and Bayesian hierarchical geostatistical modelling), so not one finding here has been independently replicated by a second study using a comparable design, which is part of why the underlying evidence is treated as incoherent rather than convergent. Temporal and Topical Mismatch: one source, Berman 2004, predates the claim's 2010-2020 window entirely, and of the remaining three, none measures funding levels directly: Lewnard 2020 measures vaccine effectiveness against illness, Bruni 2020 measures HPV final-dose coverage dropout, and only the Sbarra and Local Burden of Disease Vaccine Coverage Collaborators 2020 measles-mapping study touches funding at all, and even then only as one of four co-named drivers alongside conflict, vaccine scepticism, and supply disruption behind a documented coverage slowdown, not as an independently tested predictor of it.

name: Vaccination Coverage Equity and Health System Financing
plainQuestion: Does cutting international vaccine funding cause vaccination coverage rates to drop in low-income countries?
scope: Low and middle-income countries, 2010-2019 (one source 2004); age groups vary from under-5 children to adolescents to unspecified
metric: Immunization financing trends, HPV/MCV1 vaccination coverage rates, antibiotic-treated illness episodes prevented
aboutClaim: Only 4 real datoms were retrieved against a 100-source target, and none directly tests the claim's specific relationship (a 20%+ funding cut correlating at r>=0.5 with a coverage decline within 2 years), so confidence sits at just 11% (Speculative). The evidence split is 0 supports, 1 contradicts, 3 conditional: one 2004 source predates the 2010-2020 window, one measures vaccine effectiveness rather than funding, one documents a coverage slowdown without funding data attached, and one touches funding only as one of four co-named drivers behind a documented slowdown, not as an independently tested predictor. What is genuinely there is a real, well-documented slowdown in LMIC vaccination coverage progress after 2010, but the sources attribute it jointly to conflict, vaccine scepticism, supply disruptions, and funding, not to funding withdrawal in isolation.
